items.title: Unmasking EvilTokens: Getting to the root of device code phishing | Microsoft Security Blog
items.excerpt: Microsoft researchers dissect the EvilTokens infrastructure, revealing how threat actors exploit device code flows to bypass multi-factor authentication. The report details technical indicators, proxy configurations, and defensive strategies for identity administrators to detect and block these sophisticated OAuth abuse campaigns targeting enterprise environments.

items.title: Cloudflare participates in global operation to disrupt EvilTokens Phishing-as-a-Service | Cloudflare
items.excerpt: Cloudflare joins international law enforcement and security vendors to dismantle the EvilTokens Phishing-as-a-Service network. The operation highlights infrastructure takedown tactics, domain sinkholing, and network-level mitigations that infrastructure defenders can implement to disrupt credential harvesting campaigns at scale.

items.title: Tracking BigBear 2.0 Evilginx2 Phishing Campaign | CloudSEK
items.excerpt: CloudSEK analyzes the BigBear 2.0 campaign leveraging Evilginx2 reverse proxy technology to harvest session cookies and bypass MFA. The article provides network signatures, proxy detection methods, and identity governance recommendations for security teams defending against advanced credential theft operations.

items.title: Device Code Phishing is an Evolution in Identity Takeover
items.excerpt: Proofpoint examines how device code phishing has matured into a primary vector for identity takeover. The analysis covers attacker infrastructure, user interaction patterns, and architectural controls like conditional access policies and device compliance checks that infrastructure teams should deploy to mitigate OAuth-based credential theft.

items.title: Inside an AI‑enabled device code phishing campaign
items.excerpt: Microsoft details a campaign combining generative AI with device code phishing to increase social engineering success rates. The report outlines AI-generated landing pages, dynamic QR code generation, and detection strategies for identity defenders to identify automated phishing infrastructure and reduce user compromise rates.

items.title: Device Code Phishing: Turning a Convenience Feature Into an MFA Bypass | Trend Micro (US)
items.excerpt: Trend Micro explores how attackers weaponize legitimate device code authentication flows to circumvent MFA protections. The research provides technical breakdowns of token exchange mechanisms, network traffic analysis, and infrastructure-level mitigations including conditional access rules and monitoring for anomalous OAuth consent grants.

items.title: Three phishing campaigns abusing Vercel’s free hosting platform | Kaseya
items.excerpt: Kaseya investigates threat actors leveraging Vercel’s free tier to host phishing infrastructure at scale. The article details deployment patterns, DNS configurations, and hosting abuse indicators that infrastructure defenders can monitor to rapidly identify and block malicious web assets before they impact enterprise users.

items.title: What is device code phishing, and why are Russian spies so successful at it? - Ars Technica
items.excerpt: Ars Technica provides a comprehensive overview of device code phishing tactics employed by state-sponsored actors. The article explains the technical mechanics of OAuth device authorization flows, historical campaign patterns, and foundational defensive measures for IT teams to harden identity infrastructure against persistent threat groups.

items.title: CVE-2026-88776
items.excerpt:
Memory overflow vulnerability vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway.
This issue affects ADC: before 14.1-73.37, before 13.1-64.23, before 14.1-73.37 FIPS, and before 13.1.37.279 FIPS and NDcPP; Gateway: before 14.1-73.37 and before 13.1-64.23  leading to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or Denial of Service

items.title: CVE-2026-89136
items.excerpt: When using RPK (Raw Public Key), the client side of a TLS 1.2, 1.3 and DTLS 1.2 connection could accept an unsolicited server_cert_type=RawPublicKey which allowed a malicious or misbehaving server to bypass authentication. RPK is off by default and only enabled in --enable-rpk OR --enable-all OR --enable-distro AKA HAVE_RPK builds.
